rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is a lead tablet bearing their names and story, set into masonry at the cave entrance; Ata transmitted this from Ibn Abbas, and linguists generally say al-raqim means a book.

rows.anchor: ذهب سيبويه إلى أنها فعلى بمنزلة الذكرى، وأصلها كلوى، فأبدلت الواو تاء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الجرمي
rows.claim: Abu Amr al-Jarmi also calls it defective but treats its tāʾ as the feminine marker.
rows.anchor: وأما أبو عمرو الجرمي فذهب إلى أنها معتلة وأن التاء فيها علامة تأنيثها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu Amr's tāʾ-as-feminine analysis: the feminine tāʾ normally follows a vowel or alif and is word-final, while kiltā's tāʾ follows a still consonant and is medial; kiltā is a singular with dual meaning, and faʿlā is unattested.
rows.anchor: وشهد بفساد هذا القول أن التاء لا تكون علم تأنيث الواحد إلا وقبلها فتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If kiltā were used as a man's name, Sibawayh would make it diptote because its alif marks femininity; Abu Amr would decline it as an ordinary feminine-tāʾ name.
rows.anchor: رجلا لم تصرفه في قول سيبويه معرفة ولا نكرة؛

rows.speaker: الأخفش، الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj explain the singular verb ātat as agreeing with kiltā's singular form; agreement with its dual meaning would instead use ātatā.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: (جعل الفعل واحدا ولم يقل: آتتا, لأنه جعل ذلك لقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gardens gave their owners a complete yield without diminution; Ibn Abbas and commentators say they did not reduce it at all.
rows.anchor: ومعنى {آتت أكلها} صاحبها أكلها أي: أدت إليه ريعها تاما من غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajjarnā means we caused the water to gush forth; khilālahumā means between the gardens, whose irrigation came from a river.
rows.anchor: وأخرجنا {خلالهما} وسط الجنتين {نهرا}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, in the report through Ali ibn Abi Talha, says thamar means wealth.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية علي بن أبي طلحة في قوله: {ثمر}

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the man's thamar was gold and silver.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: (ذهب وفضة)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says he possessed every kind of wealth.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: (يقول ومن كل المال)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ: most read thamar with both vowels rounded, Abu Amr rounds the first and quiets the second, and Asim opens both.
rows.anchor: واختلف القراء في قوله: {ثمر} علي ثلاثة أوجه: ثمر بضم الثاء والميم

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says thamar is the fruit borne by a tree.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: (الثمر: حمل الشجر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamar can mean types of wealth; athmara can mean that a man's wealth increased, and thammara that God increased someone's wealth.
rows.anchor: والثمر أنواع المال، يقال: أثمر الرجل إذا كثر ماله، وثمر الله مال فلان

rows.speaker: الفراء عن مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Farra transmits Mujahid's distinction: Qur'anic thamar means wealth, while thamar means fruits.
rows.anchor: وروى الفراء بإسناده عن مجاهد قال: (ما كان في القرآن من ثمر

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd distinguishes thamar as the orchard's stock or trees from thamara as what is gathered from a fruit tree.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: (الثمر الأصل، والثمرة ما يجتنى من ذي الثمر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun thamara has several plurals, including thamrat, thimar, and thamar, by analogy with common broken-plural patterns.
rows.anchor: ويجمع ثمرات مثل: رقبة ورقبات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Amr's shortened reading can be a lightened plural of thimar, a plural of thamara, or a singular thamar; any of these analyses permits a silent middle consonant.
rows.anchor: فقراءة أبي عمرو بالتخفيف تحتمل ثلاثة أوجه أحدها: أن يكون جمع ثمار

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators say the wealthy man took his Muslim brother by the hand, led him into the garden, and showed it to him proudly.
rows.anchor: [قال المفسرون: (أخذ بيد أخيه المسلم فأدخله جنته]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the garden owner as having left faith for disbelief in God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يعني خارجا عن الإيمان إلى الكفر بالله)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says every disbeliever wrongs himself by consigning himself to the Fire, and no greater self-wrong is possible.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (وكل من كفر بالله فنفسه ظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Impressed by his thriving garden, the man foolishly denied that God could make this world perish and imagined it would last forever.
rows.anchor: أنكر أن الله تعالى يفني الدنيا، لما رأى ما راقه وكبر في نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the man denied resurrection, reward, and punishment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (أنكر البعث والثواب والعقاب)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says he disclosed disbelief in the Last Hour and in the world's eventual end.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (أخبر أخاه بكفره بالساعة، وبكفره بفناء الدنيا)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes 'if I am returned to my Lord' to mean if resurrection is true, and the man expects a better return in the next life because God favored him in this one.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد إن كان البعث حقا)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semantic authorities infer that the believer had told him the Hour would come; the man replies that, if resurrection occurs, God will give him even better because his worldly wealth shows divine favor.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: (هذا يدل على أن صاحبه المؤمن قد أعلمه أن

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the man doubted return to God yet mockingly reasoned that his present gifts must promise him something better.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: (شك، ثم قال على شكه في الرجوع إلى ربه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Of the singular and dual readings of minha, the singular is preferable because it follows the immediately preceding singular garden; the dual remains possible because two gardens were mentioned earlier.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Adam was created from dust; his descendant came from a drop, and because his father was from dust, the man too is from dust.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد أن آدم خلق من تراب)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nutfa literally means water; people call a small amount in a waterskin a nutfa, and Arabs use the term for either little or much water.
rows.anchor: ومعنى النطفة في اللغة: الماء، يقال: في القربة نطفة من ماء

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says Arabs use nutfa for both a small and a large quantity of water.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: (والعرب تقول للماء القليل والكثير: نطفة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God calls semen a nutfa, as in the verse about a drop of semen being emitted.
rows.anchor: وسمى الله عز وجل المني نطفة قال: {ألم يك نطفة من مني

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi explains 'then fashioned you a man' as making him proportionate, fully formed, and sound in limbs and senses.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (جعلك معتد الخلق والقامة, صحيح اليدين، والرجلين، والعينين)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses it as completing the man; the author prefers this because Arabic says a youth has matured and become fully grown, as in the verse about Moses reaching maturity.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (أي: ثم أكملك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lakinna is based on lakin ana, as in Ubayy's reading: the hamza is regularly lightened, its vowel moves to nūn, identical nūns assimilate, and the pause alif of ana drops in connected speech but appears at a pause.
rows.anchor: وأصله: لكن أنا، كما هو في قراءة أبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final hāʾ of pause forms likewise drops in connected speech, as in irma, aghza, and the possessive forms in al-Haqqa.
rows.anchor: كما لم تثبت الهاء في الوصل في نحو: إرمه، وأغزه،

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd transmits a comparable assimilation in a reading of 'the heaven from falling on earth': the hamza is lightened and its vowel shifts, bringing two matching lams together for assimilation.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذه القراءة في الإدغام ما حكاه أبو زيد في قول من سمعه يقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The process treats a separated sequence as connected, as in doubled forms such as shadda and halla.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله في إجراء المنفصل مجرى المتصل في نحو: شد، وحل

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، نافع
rows.claim: Ibn Amir and Nafi in al-Musayyibi's transmission read lakinna with alif in both connected and paused forms; this treats connection like pause and is not the preferred reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر، ونافع في رواية المسيبي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali offers an alternative: the nūn and alif form a connected first-person plural pronoun, not ana; nūn assimilation then explains alif in both positions, and the pronoun refers to the sense rather than the wording.
rows.anchor: غير أن أبا علي الفارسي ذكر وجها جيدا لهذه القراءة، فجعل النون والألف في {لكنا} الضمير المتصل

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says preserving alif in connection follows the dialect ana qumt; in this verse he prefers Ibn Amir's reading because the alif compensates for the dropped hamza.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق في توجيه هذه القراءة: (أثبت الألف في الوصل، كما كان يثبتها في الوقف

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq adduces a poetic line in which ana retains its alif when connected.
rows.anchor: أنا سيف العشيرة فاعرفوني ... حميد قد تذريت السناما

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali rejects Abu Ishaq's compensation: the alif is a pause marker and cannot remain in connected speech; deleted hamzas need no replacement, pronoun markers can be one or two letters, and retaining pause hāʾ as compensation would be equally required but is impossible.
rows.anchor: ورد ذلك عليه أبو علي فيما استدرك عليه فقال: (لا أرى ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The huwa in 'he is God, my Lord' is the pronoun of the affair, requiring the following clause to explain it; the same construction occurs in two other verses and was discussed at Joseph 12:77.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {هو} من {هو الله ربي} ضمير علامة الحديث والقصة،

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq infers from 'I associate none with my Lord' that the garden owner was a polytheist who worshipped another alongside God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (دل خطابه على أن صاحب الجنتين مشرك عابد مع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author characterizes Abu Ishaq's conclusion as an inference from the implication of the wording.
rows.anchor: وهذا من أبي إسحاق قول بمفهوم الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the hoped-for better gift is in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد في الآخرة)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the better gift could instead be in this world.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (وجائز أن يكون أراد في الدنيا)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Ata's report Ibn Abbas interprets the hasban sent from heaven as fire; al-Kalbi agrees.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (نارا من السماء)

rows.speaker: قتادة، الضحاك
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Dahhak gloss hasban as punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والضحاك: (عذابا)

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says hasban is a decree from God's command.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: (قضاء من أمر الله يقضيه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says these exegetical glosses capture the sense rather than the word's lexical definition; al-Akhfash defines hasban as projectiles, plural of hasbana.
rows.anchor: هذا كلام المفسرين في تفسير الحسبان، [وذلك كله معنى، وليس بتفسير. وتفسيره

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says hasban means projectiles, each one called hasbana.
rows.anchor: أهل اللغة، قال الأخفش: (الحسبان)]

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi, as transmitted by Tha'lab from Abu Amr, says hasban means projectiles; hasbana can also mean a cloud or lightning bolt.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي مما روى عنه ثعلب من رواية أبي عمرو: (أراد

rows.speaker: النضر
rows.claim: Al-Nadr describes hasban as many pointed darts shot at once from a tube, spreading like heavy rain and piercing whatever they strike; Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba give a similar account.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر: (الحسبان: سهام يرمي بها الرجل في جوف قصبة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads the threat as sending punishment that is an accounting of one's deeds, with an omitted word and hasban understood as the reckoning of sins.
rows.anchor: وجعل الحسبان بمعنى حساب ذنوبه

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari rejects al-Zajjaj's reckoning interpretation as remote and prefers projectiles of divine punishment, such as hail or stones; the author says the exegetical views also fit projectiles.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: (الذي قاله الزجاج بعيد، والقول ما قاله الأخفش وابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semantic authorities explain the name hasban by the projectiles' great number.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: (إنما سمي المرامي حسبانا, لأنها تكثر كثرة الحسبان)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cross-references hasban meaning reckoning in the verse about the sun and moon as reckoning.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا الحسبان بمعنى الحساب في تفسير قوله تعالى: {والشمس والقمر حسبانا}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says saʿīdan zalqan means land with no vegetation; al-Kalbi and others agree.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (أرضا لا نبات فيها). وهو قول الكلبي وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although zalq can mean slippery ground and a poet uses it that way, here it describes barren land, from the related sense of shaving a head: the soil is like a shaved head.
rows.anchor: والذي في الآية ليس من هذا؛ لأنه ليس أنها تفسير مزلقة، ولكن معناه: أنها تفسير جرداء لا نبات بها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra defines zalq as soil without vegetation.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (الزلق التراب الذي لا نبات فيه)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the garden's crop will have been harvested away so nothing remains.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: وفي قوله: {صعيدا زلقا} يقول: (قد حصد ما فيها فلم

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba takes zalq to mean smoothness on which feet slip; the author says smoothness is the root sense, but the verse concerns loss of vegetation.
rows.anchor: وذهب ابن قتيبة إلى الإملاس فقال: (الزلق: الإملاس الذي تزل عليه الأقدام)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened punishment destroys the garden and eliminates its yield.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أن هذا العذاب يهلكها ويبطل غلتها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the water is the river running through the two gardens.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يعني النهر الذي من خلالها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghawr describes water sinking into the ground; the same root describes an eye sunken in its socket.
rows.anchor: يقال: غار الماء في الأرض، يغور غورا، أو غوورا إذا ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis understands 'water ghawr' as 'water having depth,' with an omitted noun.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: {أو يصبح ماؤها غورا} وجهان أحدهما: ذا غور فحذف المضاف

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semantic authorities take ghawr as the adjective 'sunken,' with a verbal noun used intensively as an adjective, like calling a man 'justice.'
rows.anchor: والثاني: وهو قول جميع أهل المعاني: أن الغور هاهنا بمعنى: الغائر أقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poetic phrase describes women lamenting while standing, illustrating a verbal noun used as an adjective.
rows.anchor: نساء نائحات قائمات، فوصفهن بالمصدر.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the water will have gone away, sunk into the earth.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة في قوله: {غورا} يقول: (ذاهبا قد غار في الأرض)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owner will have no trace left by which to search for the water.
rows.anchor: أي: لا يبقى له أثر يطلبه به

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets 'you cannot seek it' as having no means or stratagem to recover it.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (لن تستطيع له حيلة)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the group that could not help the garden owner was the very retinue he had boasted about as numerous and powerful.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (لم ينصره النفر الذين افتخر بهم في قوله: {وأعز

rows.speaker: الفراء، الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj say the masculine verb agrees with the meaning of collective faʾa; agreement with the feminine noun's form would instead be tanṣuruhu, as in the verse about a faction fighting.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج: ({ينصرونه} محمول على معنى الفئة، ولو حمل على لفظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man could not recover or replace what had been lost.
rows.anchor: {وما كان منتصرا} بأن يسترد بدل ما ذهب منه.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the man could not even save himself.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (وما كان هو أيضا قادر على نصرة نفسه)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses it as being unable to protect himself.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: (وما كان ممتنعا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable concludes that the disbeliever is deceived by worldly life and expects it to last, whereas the believer patiently bears its reversals in hope of God's reward and does not rely on what he knows will perish.
rows.anchor: فالكافر تغره دنياه ويتبجح بها ويظن أنها تبقى له، والمؤمن يصبر على نوائبها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets 'there' as at that time, namely the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (يقول عند ذلك، وهو يوم القيامة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression hanalika can point either to a place or to an earlier time, as discussed at Zakariya's prayer.
rows.anchor: أنه يجوز أن يشار بهنالك إلى المكان، وإلى ما مضى من الزمان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the fatḥa form walāya, meaning allegiance or taking as a protector, the opposite of enmity; this is the verbal noun of wali.
rows.anchor: والولاية: نقيض العداوة، ومعناها التولي،

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، الأصمعي
rows.claim: Abu Amr and al-Asma'i call the kasra reading faulty here: kasra in this pattern marks a craft or delegated office, whereas this verse concerns religious allegiance; they make the same point about 8:72.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي عمرو، والأصمعي أنهما قالا: (الولاية بالكسر هاهنا لحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some linguists allow either vowel in these terms, by analogy with paired forms such as wakāla and waṣāya.
rows.anchor: ومن أهل اللغة من يقول: يجوز الفتح في هذه، والكسر في تلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With kasra on ḥaqq, the word describes God as the possessor of truth, justice, and peace; supporting phrases occur at 24:25 and 6:62, as does Ibn Masud's reading.
rows.anchor: من كسر القاف جعله من وصف الله سبحانه، ووصفه بالحق وهو مصدر كوصفه بالعدل وبالسلام

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، الكسائي
rows.claim: Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i read ḥaqq with nominative ending, making it an adjective of walāya; Ubayy's reading supports this, and the true allegiance is unmixed with rival authority or its vulnerabilities.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو والكسائي: {لله الحق} بضم القاف

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says God's protective allegiance becomes evident when He takes charge of His servant at the judgment.

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says that on that day people turn to God and believe in Him, disavowing what they worshipped; the author finds this clearer than al-Zajjaj's account.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: (يريد يومئذ يتولون الله ويؤمنون به، ويتبرؤون مما كانوا

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another view takes walāya as sovereign authority: at judgment no creature can help another, and God alone aids believers and humiliates disbelievers, as in 'Master of the Day of Judgment.'
rows.anchor: وذهب غيرهما في معنى الولاية في هذه الآية: إلى تولي الأمر، لا إلى معنى الموالاة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses yawma as an object of 'remember'; alternatively it may mean 'a better day when the mountains are moved,' but the author says that reading would be apt only without the waw.
